If the explanation of the officer is found to be unsatisfactory, the Central Government has been given the power to dismissing or removing him from service. The rule does not confer upon him the power to terminate his services. It merely confers upon the Central Govt. the power to discharge him. [452 B C]

2052: The respondents made applications under section 33 C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, praying for determination and computation of the benefit to which they were entitled under the Desai award as they were not satisfied with the fixation of their pay by the appellant bank under para 5.356 of the Desai award. The respondents contended that the respondents had no right to claim the benefit under the Desai order as they were governed by the Desai award and that the Desai award was binding on them. Held, that the respondents were not entitled to the benefit of the Desai order. The Desai order did not provide for any adjustment or revision of the scales of pay fixed by it from time to time. It merely provided for the fitment of the employees in the new scale of pay as revised by the Labour appellate Tribunal decision. The respondents were therefore not entitled to claim the benefits of the Desai orders.

3436: The appellant company was a manufacturer of arcarbons. It manufactured a series of "Cinema" and "Cinemas". The question for determination in these appeals is whether the sales of "Customs" were liable to sales tax under entry 4 of the First Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The High Court held that the sales were not covered by the entry under consideration. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the entry under the Act did not cover "welding electrodes", as defined in section 2(1) (d) of the Act, and that the entry was intended to be confined only to "the goods specified in the First Schedule." HELD: The entry under consideration does not cover "any other goods" which are mentioned in the First or the Second Schedule. [411D] The entry under the first schedule to the Act is not limited to "the articles specified in the Second or the Third Schedule" but includes "all such articles". The entry under section 2(2)(d) of Act means "every article specified in the Third or the Fourth Schedule". Therefore, the entry under section 4(3) of the A.P. General Sales Tax, 1957, is not restricted to "the article specified in any of the Schedules" and the entry under Section 2(1)(d) is confined to "the items specified in the Schedule" only. [412E F]

2727: The appellant was elected as a trustee of the temple. He took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the temple was not hereditary. The High Court held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6 sub section (9) of Madras Act 19 of 1951, and dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the appellant being a hereditary trustee was entitled to succeed to the office of trusteeship in preference to the founder who had no right to continue in management of the temple and that the suit was barred by limitation. HELD: The appellant is not a hereditary trustee but a person holding an office of profit under the Government. [839 E] The definition of the trustee of a religious institution does not include a person who has been appointed as a trustee or a member of a committee of a religious trust. The term "manager" includes a person who is in charge of the management of the trust property. [840 F G] The definition includes a person whose duties are mainly in connection with the affairs of the trust. The definition includes persons who have been appointed as trustees or members of a committee. The definition does not include persons who have taken part in the management of a trust property. The definition is not intended to cover persons who have not taken part in management of a temple. [841 B C]
3356: The accused was charged under section 302/34 IPC for having murdered the deceased. 232: The respondent was charged with various offences alleged to have been committed by him in the course of his raid as an armed gang on a certain factory known as the Jessop Factory at Dum Dum. He was convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprisonment under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Ordinance, 1949, and was sentenced to varying term of imprisonment. The respondent applied to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for the issue of a writ of certiorari quashing the conviction and sentence on the ground that the Special Court had no jurisdiction to try the case since section 5(2) of the Act provided for the speedier trial of cases instituted before or after the commencement of this Act. Held, that the provisions of section 5(3) of the Ordinance were not ultra vires the Constitution. The words "inquiry" in section 5(4) are wide enough to include all proceedings which may be taken against any person for committing or attempting to commit or abetting the commission of any offence. The words 'inquiry' in section 5 (1) do not mean only investigation but also inquiry into the conduct of persons concerned in such offences. The words used in section 5 are not confined to the stage of enquiry but they extend to inquiries into the conduct and liabilities of individuals involved in the commission of the offence. The word 'investigation ' in section 5 does not include investigation.

2440: The workmen of the appellant company were employed by the respondent company as a daily rated employee. They claimed that they should be paid minimum wages at par with those in the other concerns in the region. The Tribunal held that there was no similar industry in the region and, therefore, the question of fixing minimum wage did not arise. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the Tribunal had erred in applying the principle of industry cum-region for fixation of minimum wages and that the Tribunal committed an error inasmuch as, in making the calculation, the Tribunal merely tried to neutralise about 36 per cent of the cost of living index instead of permitting neutralisation to the extent of at least 90% which could have been done when fixing the minimum wages. HELD : (1) The Tribunal has to compare wage scales prevailing in the two regions in which the minimum wages are higher than the minimum wages payable by the Company. In doing so, the Tribunal has to take into consideration the financial position of the company, the nature of work done, the capacity of the company to pay, the capacity or the capacity of any particular class of employees to pay, and the capacity of labour to pay. [901 G H] (2) The Tribunal is not bound by the principles laid down by this Court in French Motor Car Co. Ltd. vs Workmen, ; , and the Tribunal can only consider whether the Tribunal has applied the principle of industrial adjudication in determining the minimum wages for the company 's employees. [902 A C] (3) The Tribunal cannot go behind the award and apply the principle of the Industrial Tribunal. It is open to the Tribunal to examine the merits of the matter and decide whether the minimum wage fixed by the Tribunal is justified. If the Tribunal finds that the minimum wage is not justified, it may fix the minimum wage. But if the Tribunal finds, after considering the evidence, that the minimum wages fixed by the employer are more favourable than the minimum wage prescribed by the Government, the Tribunal will not interfere with the fixation of the minimum wage unless it comes to the conclusion that the Tribunal has acted arbitrarily or unreasonably in taking the view that the minimum rate of wages fixed by it would be more favourable than what it should have.
2913: The assessee, a firm carrying on business as a contractor under the Railways, filed its income tax return for the assessment year 1960 61. 362: The assessee was the sole proprietor of a business carried on under the name and style of Indestro Sales and Service Co. at No. 50 52, Lohar Chawl Street in the City of Bombay. In respect of his own business he was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947 1948 and 1951 1952 respectively by the Third Income tax Officer, C 1 Ward, Bombay, at and for Rs. 40,178 4 0. The assessee did not pay up the assessed amount of tax within the time prescribed but filed an application before the Additional Collector of Bombay claiming that the sale proclamation issued by him was invalid as it was contrary to section 13(2) of the Act. The Additional Collector held that the sale was void because the property had been sold without notice to the assessee and therefore the sale was invalid. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Additional Collector. On further appeal the Tribunal held that the notice issued by the Additional Collector was valid. The High Court dismissed the petition under article 226 of the Constitution. Held: (i) The notice issued by an Additional Collector is not valid. It is only when the Additional Collector has given notice to the person concerned that the notice can be said to have been validly issued. The notice must be one issued by the Collector himself or by someone else. The notice should be issued by the person concerned and not by the Additional collector. The Additional collector cannot issue a notice by himself and no such notice could be issued by any other person. The Additional District Magistrate had jurisdiction to issue the notice under section 13 of the Act and the Additional Collector had no power to issue the same. [701 B D] (ii)The notice issued by a person who is not a party to the proceedings before the Additional District Magistrate is not valid because the notice was issued by the authority which passed the order. The Additional district Magistrate had no jurisdiction to issue a notice under section 14 of the Act because the notice issued was not in accordance with law. The Additional Commissioner had no jurisdiction under section 15 of the Act to issue the notices. The Additional Director of Income Tax, Bombay, was competent to issue the impugned notices. The notices were not legal and valid.
2256: The respondent No. 1 was a thika tenant of the appellant. He filed a suit for ejectment of three persons, namely, Abdul Gaffur, Abdul Hamid and Abdul Gaffar, from the property in suit (a parcel of land about 1 cottah chittaks being part of premises No. 6/1, Shibtola Lane, Entally, Calcutta). In the plaint it was alleged that the appellant had been inducted as a thika tenants by the respondent No. I under the plaintiff and the third defendant who were described as thika tenants. The suit was contested only by the third defendant and the appellant 's defence was struck off on the ground that the suit was bad for non joinder of parties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent No 1 was a tile tenant of the land and that he was not a thika or a tenant within the meaning of section 2(g) of the West Bengal Thika Tenancy Act, 1949. On appeal the Subordinate Judge held that the respondent was a thikadar and that the appellant was a thukari tenant. The High Court dismissed the second appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court rightly came to the conclusion that the respondent could not be treated as a thikadars. [174 D] The respondent was a tiny tavazhoomi tenant. The respondent was not a tinya tenant but a thika. The respondent had no right to remain in possession of the land. [175 E] The respondent had not acquired any interest in the land. The respondent could not claim to be a thika on the land. It is true that the respondent had no title to the land but the respondent was entitled to the protection of the Act. [176 F] The respondent did not acquire any interest in any land. The appellant was a tilting tavazhaoomi. The respondent did possess the land. Therefore, the respondent was not entitled to the benefit of the Act because the respondent was the thika tenant. [177 A B] The respondent could have claimed the protection of section 2 (g) of West Bengal Thikana Tenancy Act, 1950.
